question: A patient with adenoviral epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) on day 10 develops painful subepithelial infiltrates (SEIs) that blur vision. The MOST appropriate next step is:

answers.text: Prescribe topical antibiotics to prevent secondary bacterial infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Topical antibiotics have no role in viral EKC and do not prevent SEI formation; they are unnecessary here.

answers.text: Refer for consideration of low-dose topical corticosteroids under ophthalmologist supervision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Visually significant SEIs that persist beyond the acute phase may be treated cautiously with low-dose topical steroids under ophthalmologist supervision. This is the one exception to the no-steroid rule in viral conjunctivitis.

answers.text: Prescribe oral acyclovir immediately as EKC is caused by herpes simplex virus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: EKC is caused by adenovirus (types 8, 19, 37), NOT herpes simplex. Acyclovir has no role in adenoviral disease.

answers.text: Patch the eye and reassure that SEIs resolve spontaneously within 24 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Eye patching is not indicated for EKC. SEIs can persist for months and may cause prolonged visual disturbance without appropriate management.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key point: EKC = adenovirus (not herpes). The only indication for steroids in viral conjunctivitis is persistent visually significant SEIs under ophthalmologist supervision.
Correct. Persistent visually significant SEIs in EKC are the one scenario where cautious topical steroids (under specialist care) may be warranted — but avoid steroids in the acute viral phase.
